title: Tobin and the Puddle-Scared Hedgehog
markdown:
The moon, like a shiny pearl, peeked out from behind the tall Frostcap Mountains. Down below, in his snug little cottage that smelled of sleepy lavender and bubbling brews, young Tobin the wizard hummed a happy tune. A big pot on the fire puffed out soft, shimmery mist – it was his special potion for sweet dreams. Tomorrow was the exciting Starlight Market, and Tobin absolutely, positively needed a very special herb called a moonpetal for his potion. With a happy sigh, he poured the last bit of shimmery liquid into a tiny bottle with a cork.

“Ready for an adventure, Scruffy?” Tobin whispered. His eyes, bright and full of wonder, sparkled. Scruffy, a hedgehog whose quills were more of a messy tumble than a neat row, blinked his beady eyes from his spot on the rug. He gave a little snuffle, a tiny sound that meant all sorts of things. Today, Tobin guessed it meant, “Almost!” Tobin gently picked him up. His quills tickled Tobin’s chin.

But as they reached the little wooden door, Tobin stopped. Right in the middle of the path was a small puddle, catching the moonlight like a tiny fallen star. Scruffy, who usually trotted along happily, froze. His little legs wouldn’t move an inch. This was Scruffy’s funny, tricky habit: he wouldn’t walk through puddles unless you sang to him. And Tobin, who knew lots of spells, had a singing voice that was a bit… wobbly. It wobbled up and down like a little bird trying to fly.

“Oh, bother and bluster,” Tobin whispered, a puff of air escaping his lips. The market would be busy soon, smelling of yummy gingerbread and twinkling with early morning stars. He really needed those moonpetals. “Alright, Scruffy,” he said, trying to sound cheerful, hoping to chase away watery worries. “We’ll go through the Whispering Woods. It’s faster, and the path is usually clear.”

Now, the Whispering Woods, just a hop, skip, and a jump from their village, was usually a kind and friendly place. Moonbeams danced through the big, old leaves, making wiggly shadows. But because Scruffy was so afraid of puddles, Tobin had to take him the longer way. It went past the bumpy roots of the oldest oak trees and a cheerful little stream that babbled secrets.

As they got closer to the woods, the path, still damp from the night’s dew, got softer and wetter. A few more puddles lay scattered, like forgotten mirrors, dark and still. Each one made Scruffy’s quills stand up with worry. Tobin sighed, a sound as soft as a breeze through dry leaves. He tried his little song, the one he’d made just for this. “Puddles, puddles, go away, Scruffy wants to start the day… no wet toes for splashy play…” It sounded more like a creaky door than a happy tune. Scruffy just dug his little claws into Tobin’s sleeve, a silent no.

Suddenly, a rustling sound, like dry leaves skittering across stones, came from a patch of ferns nearby. Out popped a small, hunched-over figure. He had a knobbly nose that twitched with curiosity and wide eyes that looked everywhere. It was Barnaby, a goblin who collected anything that sparkled. Tobin felt a little flutter in his tummy. Goblins, he’d heard, could be tricky and liked riddles.

“Hmph,” grumbled Barnaby, his voice like pebbles rolling down a hill. “Looking for something, wizard boy? Seen any super shiny stones? Or maybe a lost earring that winks in the moon?” He slumped down, his shoulders drooping like wilting flowers. “Lost my best button, you see,” he explained sadly. “A really, really pretty, shiny blue one. Fell right off my best waistcoat. Gone like smoke.” Barnaby’s shoulders drooped so much, the trees around them seemed to sigh with him. Tobin looked at the sad goblin, his knobbly fingers tracing the worn cloth of his waistcoat. Then he looked at Scruffy, who was still trembling by a tempting puddle, as dark and still as ink. Barnaby wasn't trying to be mean; he was just truly, deeply sad.

And then, something quite unexpected happened. As Tobin watched Barnaby’s sad face, full of worry over one little button, he understood. He saw how much that small, shiny thing meant to the goblin. In his sadness, Barnaby waved his arms, his knobbly finger pointing at Tobin's bag. His hand swept across it, and out tumbled the precious moonpetal herbs Tobin had gathered! Tobin gasped. His own little seed of frustration, planted by the puddles and the late hour, started to grow. But before he could frown, Scruffy, seeing Tobin’s upset, gave a determined snuffle. With a brave, wobbly step, he walked right through the very edge of the puddle! His quills twitched bravely, and his tiny paws made a soft splashing sound. Whoooo could have guessed such a small step would be so brave?

Tobin blinked. His frustration melted away like morning frost. Scruffy was being brave. He looked at Barnaby, who was now peering sadly at the scattered herbs, his eyes wide and a little helpless. “It’s alright, Barnaby,” Tobin said, his voice soft and calm, like gentle water lapping a quiet shore. “We can find them. Don’t worry.” He remembered a smooth, grey stone he’d put in his pocket earlier. It caught the moonlight in a special, beautiful way, making it look like it held a tiny piece of the night sky. He pulled it out. “Here,” Tobin offered, holding out the stone. “Maybe this will sparkle for you? It’s very pretty in the moonlight.”

Barnaby’s eyes grew wide. His sadness lifted for a moment. He carefully took the stone, turning it over and over in his rough, dirt-stained fingers. A slow, shy smile began to spread across his face, changing his whole look. “Oh!” he exclaimed, his voice losing its grumbly sound. “It does! It really sparkles! It has the moon’s own twinkle!” He hummed a little goblin tune, a surprisingly happy, musical sound that made Tobin smile. “About those herbs,” Barnaby said, his sadness completely gone, replaced by a cheerful eagerness. “I have a very good eye for sparkle, you know. Especially after losing my button. I think I saw them tumble over there, by that old hollow log.” And with a surprisingly quick leap for someone so hunched, he pointed right to where the delicate, silvery moonpetals lay, safe among the moss and fallen leaves.

As the first hint of dawn painted the sky with soft pink and gold, Tobin and Scruffy walked back to their cottage. The moonpetals were safe in Tobin’s bag, their faint glow a reminder of their unexpected adventure. Scruffy trotted beside him, still a bit careful of damp spots, but he had walked through a puddle. He had been brave. Tobin, who had learned that a little kindness, a moment of understanding, and a shiny stone could be more powerful than any tricky spell, hummed a new, gentle tune. It wasn’t wobbly at all. It was steady and sweet. The moon, now pale and shy, a faint whisper in the brightening sky, watched them go. The ancient trees, standing tall, remembered this story well: the young wizard, the brave hedgehog, and the goblin with the lost button, all finding a bit of everyday magic in the quiet, moonlit woods.
characters: Tobin the young wizard, a hedgehog
